entries.title: Actions retention now covers checks, runs, and statuses
entries.titleJa: GitHub Actionsの保持対象にチェック、ワークフロー実行、ステータスを追加
entries.titleEn: Actions retention now covers checks, runs, and statuses
entries.contentSnippet: As previously announced , checks, workflow runs, and statuses are now governed by the same GitHub Actions retention setting that controls how long artifacts and logs are kept. These records are automatically cleaned up when they exceed the retention period configured for your enterprise, organization, or repository. This applies to checks and statuses created by GitHub Actions and third-party applications. The setting is labeled “Check, workflow run, status, artifact and log retention” in the UI. Repository retention remains subject to organization and enterprise caps, and the maximum retention for public repositories is 90 days. Changing the setting won’t restore data that was previously removed. Review or update the artifact and log retention period for your repository . The expanded retention policy applies to GitHub Actions on github.com.

entries.title: Scheduled code scanning skips inactive repositories
entries.titleJa: 定期コードスキャンが非アクティブなリポジトリをスキップ
entries.titleEn: Scheduled code scanning skips inactive repositories
entries.contentSnippet: Weekly scheduled scans for code scanning default setup and GitHub Code Quality now start only after a push or pull request triggers an analysis, rather than counting every kind of scan as recent activity. Previously, activity for a repository was based on any unscheduled scan, including the one-time validation scan that runs when you first enable default setup and scans triggered by a change in detected languages. That meant enabling default setup or rolling out a security configuration across many repositories at once could make a dormant repository look active for another six months and trigger weekly scheduled scans you didn’t expect. Enabling default setup still runs an initial validation scan and populates findings right away. Weekly scheduled scanning only begins once a push or pull request triggers an analysis.

entries.title: Code coverage uploads no longer fail CI for new branches
entries.titleJa: 新規ブランチへのコードカバレッジ送信でCIが失敗しないように
entries.titleEn: Code coverage uploads no longer fail CI for new branches
entries.contentSnippet: Code coverage uploads from the GitHub Code Quality upload-code-coverage action no longer fail CI when you push a branch that doesn’t yet have an open pull request. Previously, the coverage API required a pull request number for any push to a non-default branch. Since that number only exists once a pull request is open, pushing a new branch before opening a pull request caused the coverage-upload step to fail, even though nothing was actually wrong with your workflow. Now, when the action runs on a push to a branch without an associated pull request, it skips the upload instead of failing, and explains why in an Actions notice and step summary. This applies to: Pushes to branches that don’t yet have an open pull request. Subsequent pushes to those branches, until a pull request is opened.

entries.title: New dashboard experience now the default
entries.titleJa: 新しいダッシュボード体験が標準に
entries.titleEn: New dashboard experience now the default
entries.contentSnippet: The new dashboard experience, previously available as a feature preview, is now the default view for everyone. The redesigned dashboard helps you focus on the work that matters most and makes it easier to find and act on what you need next. You can: View your active agent sessions, issues, and pull requests in one place. Use filters to choose what appears in each section, with up to 12 items in each list. Catch up on updates in the separate Feed tab, keeping your feed distinct from your productivity-focused dashboard. Start work directly from the dashboard, such as assigning an issue to Copilot coding agent or opening a pull request in Copilot Chat. If you’d rather keep the previous experience, you can switch back at any time by clicking the dropdown next to “Preview.” We’d love to hear your thoughts on the new dashboard experience.

entries.title: GitHub async merge API generally available
entries.titleJa: GitHubの非同期マージAPIが一般提供開始
entries.titleEn: GitHub async merge API generally available
entries.contentSnippet: You can now use the generally available GitHub async merge API to merge individual or stacked pull requests, add pull requests to a merge queue, or merge pull requests directly. This includes optionally bypassing rules if you have permission. The API processes merges asynchronously, helping your automations handle busy repositories without waiting for complex merges to finish in a single request. Submit a merge request with PUT , then poll with GET using the returned request ID to check its status. The async merge API is now the recommended path for programmatically merging pull requests instead of the synchronous REST endpoint or GraphQL mutations. It’s also the only merge API that supports stacked pull requests. Check out the async merge API documentation for request parameters and examples.

entries.title: Actions Runner Controller release 0.15.0
entries.contentSnippet: GitHub Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0 includes reliability, scalability, and observability improvements for runner scale sets. These updates help you operate larger runner fleets with fewer disruptions during upgrades and Kubernetes API updates. Here’s what’s now available: Patch version upgrades now update resources in place, reducing disruption between autoscaling runner sets and ephemeral runner sets. Controller shutdown behavior is more reliable because terminationGracePeriodSeconds is configurable and now aligns with the controller manager graceful shutdown timeout. Runner scale sets can be reregistered when the recorded scale set no longer exists in the Actions service. Controller updates now use patch requests instead of full update requests, reducing Kubernetes API payload size.

entries.title: ChromebookのVS Codeで日本語入力ができない問題を解決する（code serve-web / SKK）
entries.titleJa: ChromebookのVS Codeで日本語入力ができない問題を解決する（code serve-web / SKK）
entries.titleEn: Solving Japanese Input Issues in VS Code on Chromebook (code serve-web / SKK)
entries.contentSnippet: ChromebookのLinux環境（Crostini）でVS Codeを使うと、日本語が入力できない（表示はできる）ことがあります。 原因は、VS Code（Electron）とChromeOS側のIMEプロトコルが噛み合っていないためと推測されています。 対処法としてFcitx5をインストールする方法やX11（ --ozone-platform=x11 ）を使う方法が知られていますが、私の環境ではどちらも解決しませんでした。そこで、自分の環境で有効であった方法を書き残します。 code serve-web は、VS Code本体のCLIに含まれる機能で、VS Codeをブラウザ上で動かすためのローカルサーバーを起動します。Crostini上でサーバーを起動し、ChromeOS側のブラウザからアクセスすると、VS Codeとほぼ同じ画面で開発できます。 エディタの実体はCrostini上で動き、画面だけがChromeのタブに表示されます。 なお、名前が似ている code-server （Coder社）は別のソフトウェアです。本記事では、すでにCrostiniに入っているVS Codeの code コマンドだけで使える serve-web を紹介します。 最大の利点は、日本語入力にCrostiniではなくChromeOSの日本語環境を使えることです。 画面がChromeOSのブラウザ上に表示されるため、文字入力はChromeOS側のIMEがそのまま処理します。Crostini側にFcitx5などのIMEを入れて設定する必要はありません。 また、VS Codeがすでに入っていれば追加のインストールも不要です。 Crostini側のターミナルで、次のコマンドを実行します。 続いて、ChromeOS側のブラウザのアドレスバーに次のURLを入力します。 --without-connection-token は、アクセス時の接続トークンを省略するオプションです。トークンなしで開けるので手軽ですが、認証なしでVS Codeを操作できる状態になります。
